column6: The commentary says praise precedes the human reciter and belongs to the Lord; the Psalter closes by summoning everything with breath to praise the Lord, placing the ayah's opening verdict beside a book's final doxology.

column5: all creation praises the exalted name
column6: The commentary says every created kind is a sign of its Lord; the psalm's conclusion gathers heaven and earth under praise because the Lord's name alone is exalted.
The commentary makes created kinds signs by which their Lord is known; Job tells the hearer to ask beasts and birds, which can teach this truth.
The commentary extends signs beyond human speech; Job says to speak to the earth and sea creatures, which can teach the inquirer.
The commentary says the worlds point beyond themselves to their Lord; Job asks who does not know from these creatures that the Lord's hand made them.

column5: life and breath in God's hand
column6: The commentary calls God Rabb of all worlds; Job says the life of every living thing and the breath of all humanity are in God's hand.
The commentary presents the worlds as signs of their Lord and names praise as the right judgment; this psalm asks that the Lord's glory endure and says he rejoices in his works.
The commentary reads hamd after a wicked people's destruction as a verdict on the right outcome; Psalm 104 ends by asking that sinners vanish and then turns to blessing the Lord.

column5: name praised from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary discusses the sun as a created light that can be mistaken for a deity; this psalm uses sunrise and sunset to frame praise of the Lord's name everywhere.
The commentary calls God owner of every world and develops the herd as an image; this psalm says every forest animal and cattle on the hills already belong to God.
The commentary says praise is God's due even when human speech or gratitude supplies nothing; the psalm says God would not need to tell humans if hungry, because the world and its fullness are his.
The commentary pairs the Lord of worlds with the knowledge by which created signs are recognized; Proverbs says the Lord founded earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding.
The commentary's prose brings the knowing sign-world together with the rain cloud that grows plants; Proverbs links God's knowledge to the bursting deeps and the clouds that drip dew.

column5: gods that did not create will perish
column6: The commentary's Abraham rejects setting luminaries as lords and turns to the Creator; Jeremiah's Aramaic sentence says gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish from earth and under heaven.

The commentary calls God Rabb of all worlds and contrasts the abiding Lord with transient lights; Jeremiah says God made earth by power, established the world, and stretched out the heavens by understanding.

column5: God carries Israel as a son
column6: The commentary hears in Rabb the raising of a child through successive stages; Moses recalls God carrying Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son.

column5: God teaches a child to walk
column6: The commentary's nurturing sense of Rabb is a gradual bringing to maturity; Hosea pictures God teaching Ephraim to walk and taking him by the arms.
The commentary links Rabb to nurture and the provision that brings life to completion; Hosea describes God drawing Israel with bonds of love and bending down to feed them.
The commentary develops Rabb as the one who sustains a being from its earliest state; Isaiah says God has carried the house of Jacob from birth and from the womb.
The commentary says the Rabb brings a creature through its stages to completion; Isaiah promises to carry and rescue the people even into old age and gray hairs.
The commentary says the Lord's care extends to all created kinds; Wisdom says God loves everything that exists and would not have made anything he hated.
The commentary calls God Rabb of all worlds; Wisdom says God spares all things because they are his and names him lover of life.

column5: bless the maker at natural signs
column6: The commentary develops sun, moon, stars, mountains, water, and marks as created signs; this Mishnah prescribes blessings on seeing mountains, seas, the sun, moon, and stars, directing recognition to the Maker of creation.
The commentary distinguishes the heavenly lights from the Lord they indicate; Sirach describes the stars as the beauty of heaven and an ordered display in God's heights.
The commentary says hamd can be the final word after a work reaches its limit, yet Fatiha places it at the beginning; Sirach says many words still fall short and makes God the final word.
The commentary says every world is a sign but cannot be the Lord; Sirach asks where strength can be found to praise God, who is greater than all his works.
The commentary says hamd names the full, final praise due to God; Sirach commands praise as much as possible and immediately says God surpasses it.
The commentary says each thing praises in its own language even when humans do not understand; this Jewish hymn assigns scriptural praise lines to heaven, earth, and sea as their own utterances.

The commentary distinguishes sun and rain as gifts within God's world and describes Rabb as nurturer; Jesus says the Father makes the sun rise and sends rain on both evil and good, showing provision beyond human merit.
The commentary's Rabb imagery includes the owner and sustainer of a herd; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor gather yet are fed by the heavenly Father.

column5: stones cry if people are silent
column6: The commentary says praise is already located before a human reciter and does not depend on the reader's voice; Jesus says that if his disciples were silent, the stones would cry out.

The commentary contrasts the Lord who remains with celestial bodies that set and says every good belongs at its source; James calls every good gift from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow from turning.

column5: Lord who founded earth and heavens
column6: The commentary calls the abiding one Rabb of all worlds; Hebrews addresses the Son as Lord and says he founded the earth and heavens, a Christian application of creator-Lord language.

The commentary's Abraham rejects lights that set and its later passage says all on earth perishes while the Lord remains; Hebrews says the created heavens and earth wear out while the addressed Lord remains.
The commentary's contrast is between passing worlds and the abiding Lord; Hebrews says creation will be changed like a garment while the Lord stays the same and his years do not fail.

column5: earth and fullness belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary says all praise and every good belong to the creator rather than a human possessor; Paul quotes the psalmic claim that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord while discussing food from the market.

The ayah assigns all hamd to Allah; Revelation's universal doxology addresses blessing, honor, glory, and might to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, preserving a distinct Christian account of who receives cosmic praise.

column5: only Sovereign and King of kings
column6: The commentary says Rabb without qualification belongs to the enduring Lord of all worlds; Paul calls God the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords.
The commentary contrasts the setting lights with the Lord who remains; Paul says God alone has immortality and ascribes eternal honor and power to him.
